title: Your Fridge Stales Bread 6x Faster 🍞
description:
Why does bread go stale, and why is it faster in the fridge? Stale bread isn't mostly dried out: as it cools, its starch slowly packs back into crystals (retrogradation) that squeeze out and lock away water, and that happens fastest just above freezing, so the fridge can stale bread up to about six times faster, while the freezer almost stops it and warming re-melts the crystals for a while.

topic: Why does bread go stale (even when it stays wet)?
script: Your fridge is wasting your bread. It can go stale six times faster. But why? Fresh bread is soft because of starch. In the oven, starch soaks up water, and its tight crystals melt into a soft gel. But once the bread cools, the starch packs back into crystals. Scientists call it retrogradation. Those crystals squeeze the water out, and lock it away. So the crumb turns hard, even though it's barely dried out. That's why sealed bread still goes stale. And this crystal building runs fastest just above freezing, right at fridge temperature. In the freezer, it almost stops. The fix? Warm stale bread in the oven, and the crystals melt again. It goes soft, almost like fresh, but only for a little while. So, fridge, counter, or freezer: where does your bread live?
key_facts: Staling is mainly starch retrogradation: amylose and amylopectin recrystallize and lock water away, so the loaf feels dry though little water has left (ScienceABC; McGee via Eat Your Books)
Even hermetically sealed bread hardens and stales (McGee, quoted by Eat Your Books)
Recrystallization is faster in the cold; retrogradation peaks around 0-8 °C, so fridge temperatures stale bread fastest (ScienceABC; Eat Your Books)
Bread stales almost six times faster in a refrigerator than at room temperature (ScienceABC); script says 'can ... six times' / 'up to 6x'
Freezing (below about -8 °C) almost stops staling (ScienceABC; Eat Your Books)
Reheating stale bread (e.g. in the oven) re-softens it, but it hardens again even faster afterwards (Cosmos; ScienceABC)
